title: Rise of Fascism under Mussolini in Italy (1919–1939)
tagline: Post-war Italy, the march on Rome, the consolidation of the fascist state and the road to the Abyssinian war.

overview.intro: Italy was on the winning side of the First World War yet felt cheated at the peace table, and the years that followed saw democratic government lose the confidence of much of the population. This unit covers the post-war crisis in Italy and the myth of the mutilated victory, the growth of the fasci and the squadristi violence of the biennio rosso, the march on Rome in 1922 and Mussolini’s appointment as prime minister, the gradual construction of a one-party state, and the foreign policy that culminated in the invasion of Abyssinia in 1935–36.

blocks.text: Italy had entered the war in 1915 on the side of the Allies with the promise of territory under the Treaty of London, and when the Paris conference awarded Italy far less than promised, D’Annunzio and the nationalists spoke of a mutilated victory and of a nation betrayed. The economic situation was no better: wartime inflation had eroded savings, demobilised soldiers faced unemployment, strikes shut the northern factories in 1919 and 1920, and in some areas peasants occupied the land they worked.

The political institutions were young and weak. Universal male suffrage had been introduced only in 1919, producing a parliament of fragmented parties unable to hold a coalition together, and the socialist party, the largest in the country, was split between reformists who worked within parliament and revolutionaries who followed the example of Russia. The liberal governments that had dominated the pre-war period lacked any mass base, since their system depended on patronage and local negotiation rather than party membership. The result was a parliament that could form no durable majority and a public increasingly impatient with it.

learn.title: The growth of the fasci and the squadristi

blocks.text: Fascism began in March 1919 when Mussolini organised the fasci di combattimento in Milan, bringing together ex-socialists, ex-soldiers and nationalists around a programme that was in parts republican and in parts directed against the socialists. The early fasci performed badly in the elections of 1919 and 1921, and it was their violence rather than their programme that gave them weight. Armed squads led by local bosses, the squadristi, attacked socialist and trade union offices, people’s houses and co-operatives, beat up opponents and, in the summer of 1920, extended their targets to the liberal and Catholic institutions that had supported the peasant occupations.

The period of 1920 to 1922 is known as the biennio rosso, the two red years, and the fascist response to it won the support of industrialists and landowners who feared expropriation, as well as the sympathy of the state, whose police and magistrates frequently stood aside. That tolerance was decisive: violence went unpunished, the authorities treated the squads as a bulwark against revolution, and the government of Giolitti included fascists in its lists in 1921 rather than suppressing them. By 1922 the movement had grown from a few thousand to several hundred thousand members and controlled large parts of northern and central Italy.

learn.title: The march on Rome and the coming to power, 1922

blocks.text: In October 1922 the fascist leadership planned a demonstration of force in which four columns of squadristi would converge on Rome. The march itself was farcical in military terms, with poorly armed and poorly organised columns strung out along the railways, but the political situation around it was not. The existing government had resigned, the parties could not agree a replacement, and the fascists demanded office. King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign a declaration of martial law that his ministers had prepared, and on 29 October 1922 he invited Mussolini to form a government as prime minister.

Mussolini reached Rome in a sleeping car and formed a coalition in which fascists held only a minority of the portfolios. His consolidation proceeded in stages rather than at once: the Acerbo law of 1923 altered the electoral system so that the party with the largest share would receive two thirds of the seats, and the elections of 1924 were accompanied by fascist intimidation, which gave the government a manufactured majority. When the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti publicly denounced the fraud and the violence in May 1924, he was kidnapped and murdered by fascist thugs. The murder caused a crisis in which the opposition withdrew from parliament in the secession of the Aventine, hoping the king would dismiss Mussolini, but the king did nothing, and in January 1925 Mussolini openly claimed responsibility in a speech that marks the effective end of the liberal state.

learn.title: The fascist state and Italian aggression

blocks.text: Between 1926 and 1929 the regime completed its structures: all parties and associations other than the fascists were banned, the press was censored or bought up, a special tribunal was created for the defence of the state, and the OVRA secret police monitored opposition. In 1929 the Lateran agreements with the Vatican settled the long dispute over the temporal power of the papacy and gave the regime legitimacy at home. Corporatism was presented as the third way between capitalism and socialism, in which employers and workers were organised into state corporations, though in practice it settled disputes in favour of employers and the state while suppressing independent unions.

Abroad the regime pursued aggression. Italy occupied Corfu in 1923 with little result, and in 1935 it invaded Abyssinia, a sovereign member of the League of Nations, in search of empire and prestige. The conquest was completed in 1936 with the use of aerial bombardment and gas, which were prohibited by the Geneva Protocol. The League imposed limited sanctions that excluded oil, coal and steel and that did not close the Suez Canal, so they could not stop the war and they convinced Italy that the League had no will to act. The episode drove Italy toward an alliance with Germany and Japan, and in 1936 the Rome–Berlin Axis was proclaimed, followed by the Pact of Steel in 1939 when Italy invaded Albania.

questions.prompt: State four features of the post-war crisis in Italy.
questions.answer: Four features are: the feeling of a mutilated victory, since the territory promised under the Treaty of London was not granted; inflation and unemployment that hit demobilised soldiers and small savers; waves of strikes in the factories and land occupation in the countryside during 1919–20; and weak parliamentary government, with fragmented parties unable to form a durable majority. The youth of universal suffrage, introduced only in 1919, is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each feature must be linked to the weakening of the liberal political order.

questions.prompt: Explain how the fascists consolidated their power between 1922 and 1926.
questions.answer: Consolidation proceeded in stages. Mussolini first took office in October 1922 at the king’s invitation while leading a coalition in which fascists were a minority, so he needed a parliamentary majority. The Acerbo law of 1923 provided it by awarding two thirds of seats to the largest list, and the elections of 1924 were held under fascist intimidation. The murder of the socialist deputy Matteotti after his public denunciation of those crimes produced a crisis, but the opposition’s response, the secession of the Aventine, relied on the king to dismiss Mussolini, and the king did nothing. Mussolini then claimed responsibility openly in January 1925, which marked the end of liberal government in practice. Between 1926 and 1929 the regime completed the structure with the banning of all other parties and associations, censorship of the press, a special tribunal, the OVRA secret police and the Lateran agreements of 1929, which supplied religious legitimacy.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the sequence and the failure of the opposition at each stage.

questions.prompt: Assess the results of Italian foreign policy under fascism to 1939.
questions.answer: Italian foreign policy under fascism was directed at empire and prestige, and it ended by binding Italy to Germany. The occupation of Corfu in 1923 showed the regime’s willingness to use force against a smaller neighbour, though it was abandoned under international pressure and produced nothing. The decisive episode was the invasion of Abyssinia in 1935, begun to avenge the defeat of 1896 and to give the regime a triumph at home. The conquest was completed in 1936 through aerial bombardment and the use of gas, both prohibited by the Geneva Protocol, and the League of Nations imposed sanctions that excluded oil, coal and steel and left the Suez Canal open, so they could not stop the war. The results were threefold. Italy obtained an empire it could not afford to hold, at the cost of a war that strained its resources. The failure of the League was exposed, which encouraged Japan and Germany to conclude that collective security would not be enforced. And Italy was drawn away from the western powers into the Rome–Berlin Axis of 1936, deepened by the Pact of Steel in 1939 and the occupation of Albania that same year. The judgement is therefore that Italian aggression achieved short-term prestige while producing a strategic dependence on Germany that Italy would not escape.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence of episodes, the specific weakness of the sanctions and a judgement on the strategic outcome.

questions.prompt: How far was the fascist rise to power in Italy due to the weaknesses of the liberal state rather than fascist strength?
questions.answer: The case for fascist strength rests on real capacity: the squadristi controlled whole provinces by 1922, their violence was organised and continuous, they could mobilise hundreds of thousands of members, and the march on Rome demonstrated that they were prepared to use force. But almost every step of the ascent depended on a failure of the existing order. The liberal parties had no mass base and relied on negotiation that collapsed under pressure. The king refused to sign the declaration of martial law in October 1922, and then invited Mussolini to form a government rather than let a ministry resist him. The police and magistrates repeatedly declined to act against squadristi violence, and the state treated the fascists as a defence against revolution. The Acerbo law was passed through parliament, not imposed by a coup. When Matteotti was murdered, the opposition withdrew from parliament in the hope of royal intervention that never came, and in January 1925 Mussolini could claim power because no institution was left willing to contest it. Even the 1924 majority was manufactured through intimidation that the authorities tolerated. The fascist movement was therefore necessary but not sufficient: its violence created the crisis, yet it was the neutrality of the army, the passivity of the king, the fragmentation of the parties and the inaction of the liberals in 1922 and 1924–25 that converted a street movement into a government and then into a dictatorship. A strong answer weighs both, but the sequence shows that each decisive transition was settled by a choice made outside the fascist movement.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both sides with dated evidence and an explicit judgement about which was decisive at each transition.
